newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Republican contract only partially fulfilled.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Republican contract only partially fulfilled.

text.p: The Republican-controlled Congress is about to adjourn after a two-year session with the party's "Contract with America" only partially fulfilled.

The 10-point contract was announced with great fanfare two years ago by House Republican candidates and was credited with helping Republicans take control of both the House and Senate for the first time in 40 years.
But Democrats said Republicans were trying to make Americans forget about the contract as both parties began full-scale campaigning for the Nov. 5 presidential and congressional elections.
"Contract? They never heard of it," said Senate Democrat Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakata.

In an infrequent recent embrace of the contract, Republicans rallied last Friday on the Capitol steps to mark the two-year anniversary of the contract. House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas said his party had enacted almost two-thirds of the contract provisions despite opposition by President Clinton and congressional Democrats.

"Fully 65 percent of the Contract with America is now law, including welfare reform, the line-item veto and forcing Congress to live under the same laws it imposes on everyone else," Armey said in a statement. He based his figure on enactment of 49 out of 75 provisions included within the 10 points of the contract.
Armey noted that House Republican leaders had kept their promise to vote on all 10 major items of the contract within the first 100 days of the session that began in January 1995.
Nine were passed and sent to the Senate but a proposed constitutional amendment setting term limits on members of Congress failed to get the required two-thirds majority.

Bob Dole, the former Senate Republican leader who left to become his party's presidential nominee, and other Senate Republicans did not sign on to all of the contract, but were able to enact much of it.
"We have delivered for the American people," said Trent Lott of Mississippi, Dole's successor as Republican leader.

A proposed constitutional amendment requiring a balanced annual federal budget lost by one vote in the Senate and term limits also failed. And the Senate did not pass the expanded national missile defense system called for in the contract.
Two major contract items that did pass Congress, a middle-class tax cut and a reform of product liability laws, were vetoed by Clinton and the vetoes were sustained.

Contract items that passed and were signed by Clinton: required Congress to follow its own laws and to pay for any programs it requires states to implement; gave the president authority to veto individual items in appropriation bills, crime and anti-terrorism legislation; reformed welfare and permitted Americans getting Social Security to earn up to $30,000 a year without losing benefits.
